courses.subject: UGEB
courses.title: Natural Wonders of the World
courses.description:
For many of us, the natural wonders of our planet are well known, for example, Antarctica, the Amazon Forests, the Great Barrier Reef and the Grand Canyon. Yet, few people really understand their formation and presence. This course introduces students to the concepts and processes of environmental change, such as climate change, land use change, desertification, and habitat loss.

The course adopts a scientific approach to help students understand the processes of environmental change behind some of the planet’s famous natural landscapes, landforms and natural phenomena. These shall include the natural processes (geological, atmospheric, hydrological and ecological) and anthropogenic processes (land use change, fossil fuel combustion and infrastructure development).

The course is designed around the four themes of: (i) the processes and patterns of landscape formation; (ii) the combination of natural and human-induced environmental change; (iii) benefits of natural wonders to human beings; and (iv) the methods and challenges of protecting natural wonders.

This course will cover at least three Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), namely SDG13 Climate Action, SDG14 Life Below Water, and SDG15 Life On Land. The impact of climate change on various natural wonders and related human well-being will be examined, along with possible ways to mitigate and adapt to climate change. Also, the influence of human activities on terrestrial and marine ecosystems, as well as possible options for their sustainable management will be discussed.

courses.subject: UGEB
courses.title: From Sky to Earth: A Natural Tale of the Greater Bay Area
courses.description:
The Earth is an intricate and fragile system. Slight differences in the terrain of neighbouring areas on the Earth can lead to variations in climate, geology, and marine resources. The Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) is located in the southern coastal area of China and has a subtropical climate influenced by the East Asian Monsoon. Two cities of the GBA, Hong Kong and Shenzhen, are geographically neighbours on the eastern side of the Pearl River estuary. Still, the interaction of oceanic, geologic, and atmospheric systems has shaped their local weather patterns and influenced the availability and distribution of natural resources.
This course highlights the geophysics, macroclimate, and marine science of the GBA and the microclimate in Hong Kong’s and Shenzhen’s areas. It aims to engage students in exploring the interconnectedness of the Earth and the sky through interdisciplinary subjects, thereby reflecting on human responsibilities to the natural environment, including the conservation of terrestrial ecosystems and the sustainable use of marine resources. The topics to be covered include the physics of meteorology, the principles of geology, astronomical relevance to climate, human influence on long-term climate, and natural disasters. Additionally, the course includes visiting meteorological institutions, geoparks, and high-tech marine companies.

courses.course_syllabus:
1. An Overview (2 hours)

1. Major concepts:

* Interplay of natural systems

1. Topics:

* How does the interaction of natural systems, including oceanic, geologic, and atmospheric processes occur?
* What is the interaction in the GBA?

1. The Sky (10 hours)

1. Major concepts:

* Relevance of astronomy to climate and ocean
* Basic principles of meteorology

1. Topics:

* What is solar activity and its influences on climate?
* What is the Milankovitch cycle and its consequences?
* What is the cause of ocean dynamics?
* What are atmospheric composition and its structure?
* How do energy transformations in the atmosphere influence weather patterns and stability?
* What is the cause of global wind patterns and their consequences?
* What are the features of the weather of the GBA?

1. Visit:

* Meteorological institutions

1. The Solid Earth (12 hours)

1. Major concepts:

* Basic principles of geology
* The cause of geological characteristics of the GBA

1. Topics:

* What are plate tectonics?
* What are large-scale Earth processes and formations?
* What are the composition and small-scale structures of the Earth’s materials, such as rock, mineral, and ore deposits?
* What are the features of the geology of the GBA?

1. Field study:

* On-site study of volcanic rock columns and/or rocky coastlines

1. The Ocean (8 hours)

1. Major concepts:

* Basic principles of oceanology

1. Topics:

* What is thermohaline circulation and its influence on long-term climate?
* What is ocean-atmospheric circulation?
* What is the cause of tsunamis?
* How do erosion and deposition occur?
* What are the marine features of the GBA, such as coastal features and water quality?

1. Case study of Hong Kong and Shenzhen (10 hours)

1. Major concepts:

* Understanding of natural disasters
* Basic principles of microclimate

1. Topics:

* What is the cause of natural disasters in the cities?
* What are the features of local weather patterns?
* What are the oceanic and mineral resources in the South China Sea?
* How does the natural environment influence the availability and distribution of natural resources?

1. Visit and/or seminar:

* High-tech marine companies and/or seminars on marine technology.

courses.subject: UGEB
courses.title: Experiencing and Rethinking Science and Technology in Agriculture
courses.description:
Throughout human history, we have developed different ways to strive for living in nature. Among which, agriculture is the foundation of all sedentary civilizations as it systematically provides food and other products to sustain human lives. It is an art that integrates knowledge of nature with human needs and values, evolving side by side with the development of science and technology. Today, with the advancement of scientific technology, the highly industrialized modern agriculture has greatly increased food production to support the global population growth. Yet it also brings global ethical concerns regarding sustainability, food safety, biotechnology, pollution, etc. In the past decades, increasing attention has been given to permaculture, an alternative agricultural practice that emphasizes the development of durable and self-sufficient ecosystems in farming. Permaculture is not only a practice of sustainable food production, it is also a philosophy of living with nature.

In this course, students will learn through lectures the basic knowledge about modern agriculture and its applications of science and technology; understand the fundamental principles, philosophy, and practice of permaculture; discuss the ethical issues related to the use of science and technology in modern agriculture; reflect on the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals, such as “Zero Hunger”, “Affordable and Clean Energy”, “Sustainable Cities and Communities”, and “Responsible Consumption and Reproduction”. Students will also experience the practices of modern agriculture and permaculture by making site-visits to enterprises of the agricultural industry, and to institutes practicing permaculture. Students who finish this course will be able to describe and compare the major principles and practices of modern agriculture and those of permaculture, analyze the ethical issues related to modern agriculture in contemporary societies, and formulate personal views on how to live more ethically with nature.

courses.course_syllabus:
* *There are three main topics to be covered in this course****:**

* *(1) Modern agriculture**

The following issues will be covered:

– Brief history of agriculture

The science and technology applied in modern agriculture will also be introduced, including:

– Use of machines

– Use of chemicals

– Application of biotechnology

Understanding of modern agriculture will be deepened by site-visits to modern agricultural enterprises, where students can experience the farming scale and productivity in modern agriculture.

* *(2) Permaculture**

Permaculture is an alternative agricultural practice emphasizing the development of sustainable and self-sufficient agricultural ecosystems. In contrast to modern agriculture, permaculture promotes high-science and low-technology. The following issues about permaculture will be covered:

– Basics principles of permaculture

– Philosophy of living with nature

– Practical knowledge of permaculture

Students’ understanding of permaculture will be reinforced by site-visits and hand-on practice in permaculture institutes.

* *(3) Agricultural ethics**

Modern agriculture has brought not only increased food supply, but also global concerns of ethical issues. The following issues will be covered:

– Sustainability and SDGs

– Food safety

– Biotechnology

– Pollution

Students will learn the agricultural ethics related to the use of science and technology in modern agriculture. By comparing modern agriculture and permaculture, students will be able to reflect on the ethical issues in modern agriculture and ponder on how an ethical way of living with nature can be developed. Students will also reflect on sustainability related to SDG #2 “Zero Hunger”, SDG #7 “Affordable and Clean Energy”, SDG #11 “Sustainable Cities and Communities”, SDG #12 “Responsible Consumption and Reproduction”, SDG #13 “Climate Change”, SDG #14 “Life below Water” and SDG #15 “Life on Land”. The reflection will be deepened by the site-visits to the modern farmlands and permaculture institutes, and group discussion with the course instructor and classmates.

The courses will be designed in three parts:

Part I Lectures in CUHK

– Two whole-day lectures will be given to introduce the three main topics mentioned above. Students are required to take a quiz after the lectures.

Part II Study-trip

– By experiencing modern agriculture and permaculture in real-life situations and hand-on practices, students will understand better the situations, dilemmas and ethical issues of global concern regarding modern agriculture. A six-day study-trip visiting modern farmlands and permaculture institutes will be organized to deepen students’ understanding and reflection on the three main topics mentioned above. In the study-trip, there will be site-visits, talks, practices and discussion sessions covering modern agriculture, permaculture, agricultural ethics and SDGs.

– Australia is at the top priority for the study-trip because she has well-established modern agriculture industry and permaculture practice. She is also the origin of permaculture. Taiwan is the second priority for the trip because it also has good modern agriculture industry and permaculture practice, although the scale is smaller than Australia. Due to the increasing popularity of permaculture worldwide, other countries and regions with good permaculture practices will also be considered..

Part III Seminar in CUHK

– A seminar will be organised to consolidate the ideas covered in the lectures and the study-trip. Students are required to give group presentations to apply what they have learnt in the lectures and the trip. They are required to write individual final paper afterwards.

courses.subject: UGEB
courses.title: Rethinking Environmental Protection in the Greater Bay Area
courses.description:
Environmental protection is an important part of modern civilization for the fact that human life and the sustainable development of society are based on natural resources from the environment. While there are common principles and practices for protecting the environment, local contexts might add to the intricacy between humans and their environment, and thus create multiple perspectives for intellectual pursuits. For example, cities in the Greater Bay Area (GBA) share and enjoy a lot of marine resources in the Pearl River Delta. However, coastal cities in the GBA, including Hong Kong and Shenzhen have been heavily impacted by pollution arising from rapid economic transformations and industrial developments in the last few decades. For such a global issue, concerted efforts have been made in scientific studies, implementation of international policies and strengthening of local governance to restore the damaged environment and properly manage our natural resources. Progress has been made but environmental issues remain a huge challenge to mankind.

This course aims to engage students in re-examining some current strategies for environmental protection at national, regional, local and even personal levels, by guiding them to study selected prevailing environmental problems, general practices of the society and some representative interregional collaborations in the GBA. While general principles in environmental science will be outlined, this course will focus on water resources, management of pollution in the coastal area and regional collaborations upon the issues. To gain first-hand experience in the present situation of their own city and neighbouring regions, students from CUHK and CUHK(SZ) will participate in field trips and scientific investigations. Tutorial discussions and writing assignments are learning opportunities for students to reflect on and evaluate the implementation of current environmental policies and interregional collaborations in the Greater Bay Area, in terms of the possibilities those policies and collaborations have brought, their significance and issues arising from them. The course serves as a platform across human experience and knowledge for students to exchange ideas, propose new ideas and embark on the journey to a better world as local inhabitants and global citizens.

courses.course_syllabus:
I. Basic information of Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (**lecture)**

Major concepts:

* Bay area; Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area.

Topics:

* The Past and Present of Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area.
* What can we learn from other global bay areas (Tokyo Bay Area, San Francisco Bay Area and New York Bay Area)?

II. Basic concepts in environmental science (lecture)

Major concepts:

* Natural capital; ecological footprint; ecosystem; pollution

​Topics:

* What happens to energy and matter in an ecosystem? How are our ecological footprint affecting the earth? How do we study ecosystem?
* What is pollution? How can we deal with water pollution?
* Why do we have environmental problems? What is an environmentally sustainable society? What are some major environmental worldviews? How can we live more sustainably?

III. Environmental protection in Hong Kong

(a) Environmental protection policies in Hong Kong (lecture)

Topics:

* How can we implement more sustainable and just environment policies?
* ​Review of current laws and regulations for environment protection in Hong Kong

(b) Biodiversity in the intertidal area (lecture)

Major concepts:

* Biodiversity, mudflat, mudflat ecology, biological invasions

Topics:

* What is mud? What is intertidal area?
* What are the indicators of mudflat ecology?
* What is the indicator of biological invasions?
* What is the impact of biological invasions?
* How can we use statistics to evaluate the mudflat ecology?

(c) Fisheries and Aquaculture in Hong Kong (lecture)

Major concepts:

* Aquaculture

Topics:

* Review of the fisheries and aquaculture in the context of environment issues

(d) T-Park or another site of a similar nature (field trip)

Major concepts:

* Water resources, water pollution, sludge treatment, zero waste

Topics:

* Review of the strategies of wastewater and sludge treatment in Hong Kong

(e) Oyster restoration and ecological study in Pak Nai (field trip)

Topics:

* Review of the mudflat ecology and biodiversity in the area between Hong Kong and Shenzhen

IV. Environmental protection in Shenzhen

(a) Chemical pollutants in water and soil (lecture)

Major concepts:

* Chemical pollutants, toxicity

Topics:

* The sources of pollution and the species of pollutants
* Level and toxic effect of pollutants
* Assessment, treatment and removal strategies

(b) Ecological economics, environmental protection policies in Mainland China & collaborations in GBA (lecture)

Major concepts:

* Ecological economics, regional cooperation

Topics:

* How are economic systems related to the biosphere?
* Review of the environmental policies (for water pollution, air pollution, biodiversity and marine utilization) in mainland China and Shenzhen
* The possibility, strategies and actions of collaborations in GBA

(c) Water Supplies Department in Shenzhen or another site of a similar nature (field trip)

Topics:

* Review of the strategies of wastewater and sludge treatment in Shenzhen

(d) Coral Protection Organization in Dapeng or Nature Reserve Inner Lingding Island or another site of a similar nature (field trip)

Topics:

* Review of the marine environment and biodiversity in GBA

(e) Xiangmi Park in Shenzhen (field trip)

Topics:

* Review of the low impact development strategies and biodiversity in Shenzhen city

V. Laboratory test to assess pollutants in environmental samples (lab work)

Topics:

* Pollutants assessment for some environmental samples

VI. Overall reflection and evaluation

(a) A review on the progress in environmental challenges in Hong Kong and Mainland China (tutorial discussion).
(b) Reflection on sustainable development (tutorial discussion).
(c) Regional collaboration for a sustainable future (student seminar)

courses.title: Biotechnology in biodiversity, conservation, environment and sustainability
courses.description:
In recent years, the United Nations had proposed a global plan aiming to end poverty and protect the globe, and ensure that people living on this planet enjoy peace and prosperity by 2030. The goal is going to be achieved and performed by 17 integrated subdivisions, which are also known as the sustainable development goals (SDGs). Biodiversity, conservation, environmental management, and related technologies are essential and are brought together under this bigger theme of sustainability. Biotechnology, here thus plays a great role, as it infiltrates in different part of our lives — from the food we eat to how we collect them, the drugs we take to treat illnesses, the fuel we use to power up devices and even the conservation of biodiversity and the environmental health. While biotechnology is a broad discipline that exploits different biological processes, organisms, cells or cellular components to develop new and effective technologies and is a newly emerged and an ongoing field in biological sciences, it offers opportunities to aid achieving different global matters that are happening currently or in the foreseeable future, especially issues relating but not limited to food crisis, one health, energy shortage, sustainable infrastructure and biodiversity in different habitats, etc.

This course provides a wide scope of knowledge relating to biotechnology that aims to stimulate thoughts and broaden the horizon of students from different background. It also allows the students to embrace the beauty and understand the constraint, including ethical, social, environmental and technological challenges of biotechnology. This course focuses on three major themes: 1). Introduction of the basic biotechnology knowledge of genetics and extended biotechnology techniques, 2). Showcases of the latest biotechnological developments and applications in various aspects of life sciences, 3). Discussion of key values of biotechnology and the philosophical, moral and ethical issues of biotechnology. Ultimately, this course aims at raising the awareness and promote the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) that are related to SDG#2 Zero Hunger, SDG#3 Good Health and Well-being, SDG#7 Affordable and Clean Energy, SDG#9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, SDG#11 Sustainable Cities and Communities, SDG#14 Life Below Water and SDG#15 Life On Land, to the students.

courses.subject: UGEB
courses.title: AI Meets Chemistry: Exploring the Future of Science
courses.description:
This 13-week general education course reveals how artificial intelligence and chemistry converge to transform medicine, sustainability, and everyday life. The course demystifies both fields through accessible explanations requiring no advanced mathematics.

Core Focus and Key Topics

The course centers on three interconnected themes demonstrating AI's revolutionary impact on chemistry:

AI-Powered Drug Discovery: Students explore breakthrough technologies like AlphaFold, which solved protein-folding problems and accelerates development of treatments for cancer, Alzheimer's, and infectious diseases—potentially reducing drug development from 10-15 years to months while improving global health equity.

Sustainable Materials Innovation: The course examines how AI designs eco-friendly materials, clean energy catalysts, and biodegradable plastics. Students discover how neural networks screen millions of compounds virtually, minimizing waste while addressing climate change and enabling the transition to sustainable economies.

Chemistry in Everyday Products: Students analyze molecular chemistry behind cosmetics, food, and consumer goods they use daily, understanding how AI optimizes formulations for safety and personalization—empowering informed consumer choices.

Relevance and Impact
These topics matter because AI-chemistry integration is transforming healthcare accessibility, climate crisis response, and economic development today. Students gain critical thinking skills to evaluate scientific claims and engage thoughtfully with ethical dimensions including algorithmic bias, equitable access to innovations, and technology governance. Through interactive demonstrations, dataset analysis, and collaborative projects, students develop scientific literacy to understand technological change and contribute to conversations about building a more sustainable, healthy, and equitable future—regardless of their major.

Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the 13-week course, students will be able to:

1. Explain Core Concepts: Articulate foundational principles of artificial intelligence (e.g., machine learning, neural networks) and chemistry (e.g., chemical bonds, molecular structures).
2. Identify AI Applications: Describe how AI is applied in chemistry, including drug discovery (e.g., AlphaFold), chemical synthesis, materials science, and green chemistry, using real-world examples.
3. Evaluate Ethical Issues: Critically assess ethical challenges in AI-driven chemistry, such as dataset bias, equitable access to technology, and implications for global health and sustainability.
4. Connect Science to Society: Recognize the role of AI and chemistry in everyday life, such as in consumer products (e.g., cosmetics, food chemistry), and discuss their social relevance.
5. Envision Future Innovations: Analyse emerging trends in AI and chemistry, such as lab automation and quantum computing, and propose potential future applications.
6. Apply Knowledge Creatively: Synthesize course concepts through group projects and presentations, demonstrating the ability to analyse case studies or propose innovative AI-chemistry solutions.
courses.course_syllabus:
The course introduces key concepts and real-world applications. Each week includes specific topics, activities, and references to deepen understanding.

Course Outline:

* *Week 1: Introduction to AI and Chemistry** - Understand the scope of AI and chemistry and their interdisciplinary potential

- Content: Overview of AI (e.g., machine learning, neural networks) and basic chemistry (atoms, molecules, reactions). Discussion of how AI is transforming chemistry through case studies like drug discovery and material design.

- Activities: Lecture on AI and chemistry basics; group discussion on AI’s role in science; demo of a molecular visualization app (e.g., ChemDraw or Avogadro).

* *Week 2: Foundations of Chemistry** - Build a foundational understanding of chemistry relevant to AI applications

- Content: Simplified explanation of chemical bonds (ionic, covalent), the periodic table, and molecular structures. Use of analogies (e.g., molecules as building blocks) to make concepts accessible. Interactive session with molecular visualization tools to explore 3D structures of simple molecules like water or caffeine.

- Activities: Lecture on chemical principles; hands-on activity with Avogadro software to visualize molecules; quiz on basic chemical terms.

* *Week 3: Basics of Artificial Intelligence** - Grasp fundamental AI concepts and their relevance to scientific discovery

- Content: Introduction to AI concepts: data, algorithms, supervised vs. unsupervised learning, and neural networks. Examples of AI in everyday life (e.g., recommendation systems, voice assistants). Discussion of how AI learns from chemical data to make predictions.

- Activities: Lecture on AI fundamentals; interactive demo of a simple machine learning model (e.g., predicting solubility using an online tool); group discussion on AI in daily life.

* *Week 4: AI in Drug Discovery** - Explore how AI reduces time and cost in drug discovery

- Content: Case study on AI-driven drug design, focusing on AlphaFold’s role in solving protein folding problems. Discussion of how AI predicts molecular interactions to identify drug candidates. Example: AI’s role in accelerating COVID-19 drug development.

- Activities: Case study analysis of AlphaFold; guest lecture (if possible) or video from a pharmaceutical researcher; student discussion on benefits and challenges.

* *Week 5: AI and Chemical Synthesis** - Understand how AI optimizes chemical processes

- Content: AI’s role in planning chemical synthesis routes, including tools like AutoSynthon or Chematica (now Synthia). Discussion of how AI predicts optimal reaction pathways, reducing experimental trial and error. Example: Synthesis of complex organic molecules.

- Activities: Lecture on synthesis planning; demo of a retrosynthesis tool; group activity to analyze a simple synthesis pathway.

* *Week 6: Materials Science and AI** - Learn how AI contributes to innovation in materials for energy and environment

- Content: AI in designing new materials, such as high-efficiency batteries or lightweight polymers. Case study on AI predicting material properties for renewable energy (e.g., solar cells). Discussion of AI’s role in discovering sustainable materials.

- Activities: Lecture on materials science; case study discussion on AI-designed materials; student activity to compare traditional vs. AI-driven material discovery.

* *Week 7: AI for Green Chemistry** - Explore AI’s role in promoting sustainability in chemistry

- Content: AI applications in sustainable chemistry, such as designing eco-friendly solvents or reducing chemical waste. Case study: AI optimizing reaction conditions for lower environmental impact. Discussion of green chemistry principles.

- Activities: Lecture on green chemistry; group activity to evaluate a green chemistry case study; video on AI in sustainability.

* *Week 8: Data in Chemistry: How AI Learns** - Understand the importance of data in AI-driven chemistry

- Content: Introduction to chemical datasets (e.g., PubChem, ChEMBL) and how AI models are trained on molecular data. Discussion of cheminformatics and data-driven predictions. Example: AI predicting solubility or toxicity.

- Activities: Lecture on chemical data; hands-on activity exploring PubChem; group discussion on data quality in AI.

* *Week 9: AI and Molecular Modeling** - Learn how AI enhances molecular simulations for non-experts

- Content: How AI simulates molecular behavior, including quantum chemistry simulations. Discussion of AI’s ability to approximate quantum calculations for faster results. Example: AI predicting molecular energy levels.

- Activities: Lecture on molecular modeling; demo of a simplified quantum chemistry tool; student activity to interpret simulation outputs.

* *Week 10: Ethical Considerations in AI and Chemistry** - Critically analyze the ethical dimensions of AI in science

- Content: Ethical issues in AI-driven chemistry, including bias in datasets, equitable access to AI tools, and implications for global health (e.g., drug affordability). Case study: AI in developing drugs for neglected diseases.

- Activities: Lecture on ethics; group debate on AI’s societal impacts; reflective essay assignment.

* *Week 11: AI in Everyday Chemistry** - Connect AI and chemistry to everyday life

- Content: AI applications in consumer products, such as personalized cosmetics or food chemistry (e.g., flavor optimization). Discussion of AI in quality control and product formulation. Example: AI designing fragrances.

- Activities: Lecture on consumer chemistry; case study on AI in cosmetics; group activity to design a hypothetical AI-driven product.

* *Week 12: Future Trends in AI and Chemistry** - Envision the future of AI and chemistry integration

- Content: Emerging trends, such as AI-driven lab automation (e.g., robotic labs) and quantum computing in chemistry. Discussion of speculative applications, like AI designing novel molecules for space exploration. Student-led exploration of future possibilities.

- Activities: Lecture on future trends; student brainstorming session on AI-chemistry innovations; preparation for final presentations.

* *Week 13: Student Presentations**

- Content: Students present group projects on a chosen AI-chemistry topic (e.g., a case study, hypothetical application, or ethical analysis). Course review, reflecting on key learnings and future implications. Final quiz covering key concepts.

- Activities: Student presentations; class discussion on project findings; final quiz (concept-based, no advanced math).

courses.subject: UGEB
courses.title: Origins – From Cosmos to Life
courses.description: The course aims at providing an introduction to the formation of the cosmos and the origin of life from an astrophysical perspective. The journey starts from the origin of the universe, and leads us through all the intermediate milestones such as the appearance of matter, the formation of galaxies, the formation of stars and planets, the appearance of simple life forms, and the evolution of life on Earth. Students can thus develop a complete picture of the current understanding of the emergence of life in the cosmos, and gain perspectives of the scientific method that allows us to arrive at the knowledge.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for Physics Majors; students in the following concentration area of Natural Sciences Programme: Physical Sciences; and students who have taken PHYS2401, 2910, UGEB2401, 2411 or 2510.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.course_syllabus:
The course will start with an overview of the formation of the cosmos, the subsequent important events in the history of the universe, and the origin of life. The important milestones include
1. The origin of the cosmos.
2. The appearance of the basic form of ordinary matter (protons, neutrons, and electrons) and light elements.
3. The formation of astronomical structures (galaxy clusters, galaxies, stars).
4. The appearance of heavy elements in various stages of star evolution.
5. The formation of planets.
6. The appearance of simple and complicated molecules.
7. The emergence of elementary life forms.
8. The process of evolution on Earth and history of life.
The brief overview of all these steps will provide the students with a mental map of how different pieces fit into the big picture.

Then some of the major topics will be discussed in depth. For each of those chosen topics, the discussion will be about what the latest understanding is, and how we arrived at the understanding. The latter part will focus on the logical arguments in understanding observations and experiments, so that the students can develop a solid understanding of how scientific method is applied throughout the process.

In particular, the topics which would be covered in depth are Topics 1, 3, 4, 5, and 8. They are chosen because we understand them the best, and because all of them can be explained in relatively simple way to non-experts.

Finally, the course will cover some latest developments of the research on the various steps. Some of the results could be more speculative, and would lead to some open questions for the students. If time permits, the course will also cover some topics about the implications of the whole “story”, e.g., are we alone in the universe?

courses.subject: UGEB
courses.title: Chemistry in Action
courses.description: This course is designed for students with minimal background in Chemistry to acquire some general chemical knowledge related to our daily lives. The main objective is to acquaint students with some scientific background knowledge in chemistry. Students will be able to read about science and technology with some degree of critical judgment. This knowledge is essential for students to solve some problems in daily lives, such as to choose the right products and to compare the risk and benefits in some cases. This course will emphasize practical applications of chemistry to problems solving such as environmental pollution, energy resources, and human health. Some demonstrations will be carried out during classes.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for stud major in prog by Fac of MED;not for Chem;students in the con. areas of NatSciProg: AnaTestSci;or ChemSci; students taken CHEM2382,UGEB2370,2380,2420or2440.Co-requisite:UGFH1000,UGFN1000or1001(only applicable to stud admitted to 4year curri)
courses.learning_outcomes: The students in this course will learn some general chemical knowledge related to the environment and the products they encountered in their daily lives. Through this learning, the students will understand the world we live, our environment, and our body. The students will be able to do critical thinking and comparing the risks and benefits in daily Life.
courses.course_syllabus:
Week 1

Introduction

Some general chemistry concepts will be taught, such as chemical bonding, concentration of a solution, brief introduction of atoms, elements and molecules, some organic compounds.

Week *2*

Fitness and Health

Athletic performance, nutrition, vitamins, minerals, muscles, exercise, sports materials.

Week 3

Oxidation and Reduction

General concepts of oxidation-reduction, with examples in cut-apple, egg cooking, corrosion, photography, battery, breathalyzer used in road blocks, explosives. Demonstrations: Chemiluminescence, potato battery.

Week 4

Acid and Bases

Acid strength, pH values of some common substances, common acids and bases, phosphoric acid, household products with acids or bases, neutralization reactions, antacids, acid-base buffers, the blood system, acidosis, alkalosis.

Demonstrations: Red cabbage extract - the natural indicator

Week 5

Chemistry of Household Chemicals

The chemistry of surfactants, soaps and detergents, stain removal, bleach and whiteners, chemicals in dry cleaning, corrosive cleaners.

Week *6*

Chemistry of cosmetics and haircare products

The general chemistry of cosmetics and toiletries, creams and lotions, lipsticks and powders, sunscreen products, perfumes, deodorants, shampoos, hair perm, hair dyeing.

Demonstration: ingredients in creams and lotions

Week 7

Food Additives

Food preservatives, antioxidants, sequestrants, food flavours, food enhancers, pH control in foods, anticaking agents, stabilizers and thickeners.

Demonstration: food colouring and other food additives

Week 8

Mid-term examination

Week 9

Toxic Substances

Poisons, lethal dose, corrosive poisons, metabolic poisons, neurotoxins, teratogens, mutagens, carcinogens

Week 10

Drugs

Development of medication, pharmacies, hormones used in sport, over the counter drugs, hallucination drugs, anticancer drugs, nicotine and tobacco, drug interaction

Weelk 11

Chemistry of the Environment

Greenhouse effect, acid rain, ozone depletion, air pollutants, hazardous waste.

Video show: "Ozone depletion"

Week 12

Energy and resources

Gasoline, diesel, natural gas, solar power, hydroelectric power, wind power

Week 13

Materials - Polymers

Polymers, Natural fibres, synthetic fibres, paints and adhesives, plastics and polymers
